deep.reconstruction:
Context. The previous page is a family letter dated Göttingen, 26 April 1857. The next page has a draft covering letter to a journal editor (Crelle/Borchardt) and a draft of the Dirichlet-principle argument: the integral Omega is finite and non-negative, so it has a minimum. This page is therefore a draft of the opening of Riemann's 'Theorie der Abel'schen Functionen' (J. reine angew. Math. 54, 1857).

(a) Heavily cancelled header. It reads roughly '[Anwendung] des Abel'schen Additionstheorems zur Integration eines Systems von Differentialgleichungen nach Jacobi (Crelle J. Bd. 9, [1832])'. This refers to Jacobi's 'Considerationes generales de transcendentibus Abelianis' (Crelle 9, 1832). There Jacobi uses Abel's theorem to give the algebraic integrals of a system of the form sum_i x_i^k dx_i/sqrt(X(x_i)) = 0 (k = 0..p-1). That formulation leads to the Jacobi inversion problem. Riemann tries several wordings ('Ich beschränke mich dabei auf das [Additionstheorem] ...') to limit his treatment to what the paper needs.

(b) Title: 'Theorie der Abel'schen Functionen v. B. Riemann.' Methodological sentence: he will develop the subject only as far as the applications in this paper require.

(c) The mathematical kernel. This is the first step of Riemann's proof of Abel's addition theorem.
- Let the algebraic function s(z) be defined by F(s,z)=0 with mu branches (a mu-sheeted surface over the z-plane).
- Let omega = ∫ R(s,z) dz be an Abelian integral, R rational.
- Let omega^{(1)}, ..., omega^{(mu)} be its values on the mu sheets over the same z.
- Then d omega^{(1)} + ... + d omega^{(mu)} = sum_i R(s_i,z) dz. [mine] This sum is symmetric in the roots s_i of F(.,z)=0, so it is a rational function phi(z) dz.
- Partial fractions [mine] give: ∫ phi(z) dz = (rational function of z) + sum_k c_k log(z - a_k) + const.
- So omega^{(1)} + ... + omega^{(mu)} equals a rational function plus logarithms of rational functions of z, determined up to an additive constant.
- The draft first writes 'Logarithmen algebraischer Functionen' and then rephrases this as 'rationaler Functionen von z'. Both are correct, the a_k being algebraic constants.
- [mine] For an integral of the first kind (finite everywhere), the rational and logarithmic parts vanish, so the sum is constant.
- The page breaks off at 'und zwar als Summe von ...'.

In the printed paper the same argument is carried out with z replaced by an arbitrary rational function xi of (s,z). One sums over the m points where xi takes a given value. This yields Abel's theorem in Riemann's form.
errors: No mathematical errors visible; the argument is only begun.

'Logarithmen algebraischer Functionen' is looser than the precise statement: logarithms of linear factors z - a_k with algebraic a_k, i.e. of rational functions of z over an algebraic extension. Riemann himself appears to correct this to 'rationaler Functionen'.
The symmetric-function step (sum over branches is rational in z) is not stated explicitly; it is standard.

results.what: The sum over all sheets of an Abelian integral at the same z equals a rational function plus logarithms, determined up to a constant; for first-kind integrals the sum is constant.
results.modern_name: Abel's theorem (trace/norm form: the trace of an Abelian differential under z is a rational differential on P^1)
results.usually_credited_to: N. H. Abel (1826/1841); Riemann's formulation appears in Theorie der Abel'schen Functionen (1857)

results.what: Reference to Jacobi's use of the addition theorem to integrate a system of differential equations
results.modern_name: Jacobi's formulation of the inversion problem via Abel's theorem

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of the opening and the Abel's-theorem argument of Riemann's published 1857 paper. It has biographical and editorial interest (dating, wording variants, an explicit nod to Jacobi 1832) but no new mathematics.

checkable.asserts: On s^2=z^3+1, the sum over both sheets of R(s,z)=(z+s)/(s-1) is a rational function of z, (2z^3+2z+2)/z^3. Should give 0 after substitution.
The sum of the branch integrals is a rational function plus constant, here with no logarithmic part. Should simplify to 0.
For the 3-sheeted curve s^3=z^2+1, the sum of the branches s_i is 0. Hence ∫(s_1+s_2+s_3)dz is constant, a trivial instance of the claim.

The sum over sheets of 1/(s-z) on s^2=z^3+1 is the rational function 2z/(z^3-z^2+1)... i.e. -2z/(1+z^3-z^2) up to sign. Its integral produces logarithms of rational functions of z with algebraic roots.

transcription_corrections: Header '(C. J. Bd. 9. p 30 S. 32. S. 8.)': the '32' is most likely the year, i.e. '(C. J. Bd. 9. p. 39[4?] 1832 ...)', referring to Jacobi's Considerationes generales de transcendentibus Abelianis, Crelle 9 (1832).
First words: probably '[Anwendung] des Abel'schen Additionstheorems ...'; the cancelled word before 'Additionstheorems' looks like 'Integrales/Integration'.

'ω_1^{(1)}, ω_2^{(2)}, … ω_μ^{(μ)}' should probably read ω^{(1)}, ω^{(2)}, …, ω^{(μ)}: the values of one integral on the μ sheets over the same z. The apparent subscripts are likely stray marks or a cancelled index.
'{+Ergibt sich+} wenn' is uncertain; the inserted word may be 'Bezeichnet' or similar.

'eine Summe [...] und Logarithmen algebraischer Functionen' is followed by a reformulation 'rationaler ... Functionen von z bis auf eine Constante bestimmt'. Read: 'a sum of rational functions and logarithms of rational functions of z, determined up to a constant'.

'Ich werde in diesem Gegenstand nicht hier nur weiter entwickeln' is better read as 'Ich werde in dieser [Abhandlung] den Gegenstand nicht weiter entwickeln, als die in dieser Abhandlung zu machenden Anwendungen erfordern'.
